plan_turns.user: I'm not really sure what I've got, honestly. My wife Carol handled all the money stuff until she passed last year. I'm 64 and an engineer in Virginia. Can you tell me if I can stop working at 66? What would it take to make that work?
plan_turns.text:
I am sorry about Carol. Based on your plan, retiring at 66 falls short. Your plan shows you have no savings now, so the plan starts from zero. Your spending goal is $44,000 a year. The plan's safe spending is $37,500 a year, a gap of $6,500 a year. The plan pays the basic costs of $40,000 a year in only 24 of 100 simulated runs, so the basics are not covered in most cases. Your plan also shows a $14,000 shortfall for an emergency fund of three months of spending.

To close the gap, the plan's figures point to saving more. You now save $7,500 a year. At ages 60 to 63, the 401(k) catch-up limit is $11,750 a year, and the total 401(k) limit for people 50 and older is $34,000. Waiting to claim Social Security past 66 raises the benefit, up to age 70. Your plan uses a claim age of 66. Social Security survivor benefits for a widower can start as early as 60, but full survivor benefits at 66 are listed at $31,100 a year in your plan.

Please talk with a fee-only financial planner or a tax professional soon. They can check Carol's accounts, life insurance, and Social Security records, and they can test a later retirement age.
